timeline.means: Episode 3 of lerobot/pusht, 159 of its 159 timesteps, on one axis. Tracks: action, observation.state, next.reward, next.success, next.done. Every series is indexed by the SAME `t`, which is the point — two series read off two panels with two x-ranges is how a coincidence gets asserted that is not there. This dataset publishes no unit for action, observation.state, next.reward, next.success, next.done, so those axes are in whatever the recording used. Two tracks with no units cannot be compared to each other, only to themselves over time.

reference.row_span_from: meta/episodes `dataset_from_index`, the dataset's own row map
reference.metric: Mahalanobis distance from the mean of 12746 rows of `observation.state`, over the 2 of 2 directions that reference set varies in

distances.percentile_method: nearest rank over every reference distance, held exactly — these are not read off the histogram below, which exists for drawing

reference.null_position_caveat: these two percentiles are not the same quantity and are not expected to agree: `null_covers_percentile` is 100*K/(K+1) from the draw count alone, while `null_max_percentile` is where the measured maximum landed among the reference distances. They are also not measured under the same conditions — the reference distances are IN-SAMPLE (the mean and the covariance were fitted on those very rows) while every null row is OUT of that fit, so the null's distances run a little larger for that reason alone. Reading the expected figure as the measured one overstates how ordinary the null was.
reference.null_description: the largest distance reached by 255 row(s) of `observation.state` drawn from this same dataset, none of them in the reference set and none from episode 3.

ood.means: Episode 3 of lerobot/pusht, 159 of its 159 frames scored at stride 1. THE REFERENCE SET IS 12746 ROWS of `observation.state` from this same dataset — every 2th eligible row of 25491 eligible, out of 25650 carrying the column and 25650 in the snapshot. The distance is Mahalanobis distance from the mean of 12746 rows of `observation.state`, over the 2 of 2 directions that reference set varies in, so it is in units of that reference set's own spread and nothing else. This episode's own 159 rows were held OUT of the reference set, its mean, its covariance and its null — a frame compared against a distribution it helped define is partly measuring itself. The furthest frame is t=110 at 2.5764, which is the 98.486th percentile of the reference distances (one row of the sample is 0.008 of a point, and that is the resolution). THE NULL: the largest distance reached by 255 row(s) of `observation.state` drawn from this same dataset, none of them in the reference set and none from episode 3. It reached 2.8067, which sits at the 99.561th percentile of them (99.561, read off the 12746 reference distances themselves rather than assumed). The maximum of 255 draws is EXPECTED near the 99.61th percentile — that is the null's own resolution, and raising `null_draws` is what sharpens it, but it is a figure from the draw count and not a reading of this null. NONE of the 159 scored frames beat it: on this evidence no frame of this episode is further from the dataset's centre than rows drawn from the dataset itself get. THE RANKING IS CAPPED: `ranked` holds the 20 furthest of 159 scored frames. Every one of the 159 is in `frames`, in time order — the cap is on the ranked listing only. A DISTANCE IS NOT A VERDICT. Nothing here is labelled out-of-distribution, because that word is a threshold and this reports a distance, its percentile in a named reference set, and whether it beat a measured null. And it is a distance in `observation.state` ONLY: a frame that is visually bizarre while its recorded vector sits in an ordinary place reads as ordinary here, and no vision model was run.

ood_cost.forward_passes_why: nothing here runs a model. No vision tower, no action expert, no GPU, no `av`, and no lerobot sidecar — the reference set is the dataset's own recorded vectors and the distance is arithmetic over them. The cost is parquet rows read, below.
ood_cost.passes_why: the first pass measures the reference mean and covariance, the second measures every reference and held-out null row's distance against them — the metric has to exist before a distance in it can. Twice the I/O for a constant amount of memory, the same trade `dataset_action_stats` makes. The episode's own rows are then read once more, from the shards it lives in only.
ood_cost.readability_why: `reference_rows` and `null_draws` are counted from the parquet footers, which carry row counts and column names but not row contents. A malformed row — not a list, the wrong width, or holding a non-finite value — cannot be seen from a footer and is dropped by the run, so both figures are ceilings rather than predictions. The run reports what it actually folded in as `rows_read` and what it threw away as `rows_malformed`; if those two do not add up to this number, the difference is malformed rows and is named there.
ood_cost.row_span_from: meta/episodes `dataset_from_index`, the dataset's own row map
ood_cost.peak_basis: one arrow batch of 8192 rows at 264 bytes a row (a 2-value row is 80 bytes of Python floats and list slots on 184 bytes of list overhead, MEASURED with tracemalloc rather than assumed), a 2x2 float64 covariance accumulator, 12746 float64 reference distances (doubled for the concatenation that sorts them), and 159 episode vectors at the same per-row rate. The arrow buffer under the batch and the torch tensors are outside the Python heap and sit on top of this.
ood_cost.seconds_from: not estimated — this is disk-bound, nobody has timed this machine's parquet reads, and a duration from somebody else's disk is a number people plan around
